newsitem.title: INDIA: India's new market rules unlikely to lift gloom.
newsitem.headline: India's new market rules unlikely to lift gloom.

text.p: New rules on short-selling announced by India's market regulator are unlikely to lift depressed stock markets, brokers said on Tuesday.
Some branded the move as over-regulation and said the new rules were likely to hit trading volumes.
The Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI) on Monday announced steps aimed at regulating and increasing liquidity in the stock markets.
"Yes...the new rules will curb short-selling to some extent, but this seems to be over-regulation on the part of SEBI," Ulhas Paymaster, a member of the Bombay Stock Exchange, told Reuters.
SEBI chairman D.R. Mehta told reporters after a board meeting in New Delhi that short-sellers would have to report their short sales position at the end of each day.
"This does not make the markets any better...all this shows is that they are laying emphasis on wrong factors," said a leading broker who did not wish to be named.
He said the new rules would only further depress the market.

"Occasionally there are cases of bear hammering. Action of this kind would prevent such incidents occurring," SEBI chairman D.R. Mehta told Reuters after a news conference on Monday. "We are performing our role as a regulator."

Concerns over political stability after a loose 13-party coalition government was formed last June, a liquidity crunch and a disappointing 1996/97 budget have dragged shares down in the past four months, analysts said.
The benchmark 30-share index of the BSE has crashed about 935 points or nearly 23 percent from the year's peak of 4,069 on June 18. The index ended at a provisional 3,134.08 on Tuesday.
Sunil Kothari, chief of brokerage Nagindas Kothari, said he did not expect the new curbs on short-selling to make a big difference to market sentiment.
"When there will hardly be any speculation, trading volumes are bound to dry up...," Kothari said.
An analyst at a local brokerage said the new guidelines would help prevent recent rampant short-selling in pivotal stocks.
"However, the broader market will not be greatly affected by the new rules," the analyst said.
A severe lack of confidence among retail investors was one of the major factors affecting stock markets, brokers said.
